Short answer up front: according to the Westminster Standards you should not set up representational images of the persons of the Godhead as aids to worship. The Standards read the second commandment as forbidding making representations of God and forbidding the worship of God by images or any other way not appointed in Scripture. So Aaron’s apparent “feast to the LORD” does not overturn the command; the Standards treat representations of God as illicit even when intended to honor the true God.

Key citations (Westminster texts and exact wording)

- WSC Q99 (Which is the second commandment?) — the Catechism quotes the commandment itself (Exod. 20:4–6):
  "The second commandment is, Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, nor the likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the waters under the earth; thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them..."

- WSC Q100 (What is required in the second commandment?) — the Catechism’s plain application:
  "The second commandment requireth the receiving, observing, and keeping pure and entire, all such religious worship and ordinances as God hath appointed in his word; and forbiddeth the worshipping of God by images, or any other way not appointed by him."

- WCF, Chapter XXI, paragraph I (on religious worship) — states the governing principle about how God must be worshipped:
  "The light of nature showeth that there is a God, and that he is Lord and Judge of all; yet . . . the acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men, or the suggestions of Satan, under any visible representation, or any other way not appointed in the Holy Scripture."

How these texts bear on your specific proposal

- The Shorter Catechism explicitly forbids “the worshipping of God by images, or any other way not appointed by him.” That covers not merely idolatrous worship of foreign deities but any use of images as a means of worship. The Confession’s general principle (WCF XXI.1) explains that worship must be performed only in the way God has appointed, and that he must not be worshipped “under any visible representation.” Put together, the Standards do not draw the permissive line you suggest (i.e., “it’s only idolatry when folks mean a different god”); they treat representational imagery of God as an illicit form of worship even when intended for the true God.

- The Aaron example in Exodus is historically a proof that external forms can be misused; the Standards see the command as preventive of that kind of misuse and as a positive rule about how God is to be worshipped. The fact that Aaron called it “a feast to the LORD” does not make a representative image an acceptable means of worship from the Westminster perspective.

Practical counsel consistent with the Standards

- Do not install a cast‑bronze “Christ in Glory” on the platform as an aid to worship, nor place icon‑style panels of the Father, Son, and Spirit in a prayer room if they are to function as objects of devotion or visual foci for worship. The Standards treat such representational depictions of the persons of the Trinity as incompatible with the way God has appointed worship.

- If you want visual help for devotion that is consistent with the Standards, prefer non‑representational and Scripture‑centred options: the cross, Scripture text art, symbolic motifs (light, lamb, shepherd imagery where the symbol points to biblical truth rather than attempts to depict the person of God), stained glass Bible scenes that direct attention to Scripture rather than portraying the Trinity as an object of devotion, or art that helps teach biblical truth without making a material representation of the persons of the Godhead.

How to read Luke 14:26 in the light of the Westminster Standards (summary)
- Christ’s supremacy: The Standards teach that God’s glory and our relation to him is the supreme duty. You may rightly be called to put Christ before all, even if that brings suffering. (This is the point WSC Q1 expresses.)
- “Hate” as comparison, not vindictiveness: Reformed tradition (and the Standards’ general theological method) treats Jesus’ strong language as requiring a decisive preference for Christ over family, possessions, and self. It does not teach that a disciple should practice malicious hatred or refuse the biblical duties that flow from God’s law.
- Duties to parents remain: The moral law still binds Christians to honour and care for parents. That obligation is not nullified by a call to missionary service unless parents command that which is contrary to God. The Christian must balance obedience to lawful parental authority (especially if dependent) with obedience to God.

Practical counsel in your situation
1. Test the claim that cutting contact is required. Ask your leaders: exactly what text or theological principle makes no‑contact obligatory rather than a last resort? Radical discipleship must still be ordered by Scripture: Christ’s call to follow is radical, but it does not abrogate the fourth commandment’s demands to honour parents unless the parents require that which is sinful.

2. Honour while following Christ. Practically, that often looks like:
   - Patiently and respectfully explaining your sense of call to your parents.
   - Setting firm but loving boundaries for conversations that become manipulative or guilt‑trips.
   - Continuing to care for their needs and to show filial respect, even when you refuse to be steered away from gospel work.
   - Seeking to win them by Christian conduct and prayer, rather than escalating conflict.

3. If your house leaders press for literal “no contact,” press them to justify that step biblically and pastorally. Absolute severance is appropriate only where continuing contact would cause you to sin, or where there is abuse, persistent hindrance to your ability to obey Christ, or a situation in which contact facilitates ongoing sin. Even then, explain your reasons to them and to your parents with humility and love when possible.

4. Use wise outside counsel. Bring this situation to a pastor or session elder who will weigh both commitments — Christ’s supremacy and filial duty — under Scripture and the Standards. The Westminster Standards value ecclesiastical oversight and prudence in matters of conscience and relational duty.

The Westminster Standards (Confession and Catechisms) build on those biblical texts and treat those attitudes as sinful and contrary to Christian duty. Key biblical passages that treat contentment as duty and murmuring/envy as sin
- Philippians 4:11–13 — Paul: “I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.” (Paul treats contentment as a learned, moral habit rooted in Christ.)
- 1 Timothy 6:6–10, 17–19 — “godliness with contentment is great gain”; warns the love of money is the root of many evils and urges the wealthy to be generous and content.
- Hebrews 13:5 — “Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.”
- Philippians 2:14 — “Do all things without murmurings and disputings.” (Paul commands Christians to avoid grumbling.)
- 1 Corinthians 10:9–11 — Paul cites Israel’s murmuring and warns Corinthians not to follow that pattern (“Neither let us tempt Christ, as some of them also tempted, and were destroyed of serpents.” and later “Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer.”)
- Numbers 11; Exodus 16; the wilderness narratives — Old Testament examples showing God treats murmuring and ingratitude as sin (examples to warn the church).
- James 3:14–16 and James 4:1–3 — envy, selfish ambition and quarrels are sinful and stem from sinful desires.
- Psalm 37 (esp. vv. 1–11) and Proverbs 14:30, 23:4–5 — wisdom literature warns against envy and anxious striving after wealth and honors.
- Luke 12:15 and the parable of the rich fool — warns against covetousness and seeing life as measured by possessions.

How the Westminster Standards approach the issue (summary, with where to look)
- General principle: The Standards repeatedly say that Christian obedience consists of both negative duties (abstaining from sin) and positive duties (practicing grace). Contentment is treated as part of the Christian’s duty of sanctification and right obedience to God’s law and gospel. Conversely, murmuring, covetousness, envy, and ungrateful complaining are classified as sins to be mortified.
- Where the Standards ground this:
  - The Confession’s treatment of the Law and the believer’s duty to obey God’s moral law shows that attitudes (heart sins) are included under the commandment’s requirements. See the Confession’s chapters on the Law of God and on Sanctification/Good Works for the general framework that inward dispositions are required to be conformed to God’s will.
  - The Larger and Shorter Catechisms, when treating the Ten Commandments and particular sins to be mortified, list covetousness, envy, murmuring, and unthankfulness among the sins forbidden and duties required. The catechisms also treat contentment as a Christian virtue tied to trust in God’s providence and the gospel.
  - The Standards also quote and appeal to the biblical texts listed above in their proofs and explanations of duties and sins.

Pastoral application and a practical note for your session
- Teach contentment as a commanded Christian duty rooted in Scripture (Philippians, 1 Timothy, Hebrews). Emphasize both the negative (do not murmur, do not envy, do not covet) and the positive (cultivate thankfulness, trust in God’s promise, practice generosity).
- Use biblical examples (Israel in the wilderness; Paul’s example) and pastoral counsel (prayer, Scripture-meditation, corporate mutual exhortation) to show how to put contentment into practice.
- Distinguish Christian contentment from Stoicism: Stoicism prized apatheia and self-sufficiency. Christian contentment is explicitly gospel-shaped — it rests on God’s promises (e.g., “I will never leave thee”) and on union with Christ (Philippians 4:11–13), not merely self-mastery.

Short answer first: the Westminster Standards require that Christian prayer be offered “for things agreeable to his will” and that God orders all things by his providence. That means you must not bless a practice that treats Matthew 18:19 as a magic formula that “guarantees” any specified earthly outcome when two people merely agree verbatim. Teach the prayer team to pray in faith and unity, but also in humble submission to God’s will and under the doctrine of providence. Remove “guaranteed” labels and correct the teaching that “if it be thy will” is unbelief.

Grounding and proof-texts from the Standards (quoted):

- What prayer is: WSC Q98 — “What is prayer? Prayer is an offering up of our desires unto God, for things agreeable to his will, in the name of Christ, with confession of our sins, and thankful acknowledgement of his mercies.” (Shorter Catechism Q98)

- The rule for prayer: WSC Q102 — “What rule hath God given for our direction in prayer? The whole Word of God is of use to direct us how to pray; ... but the special rule of prayer is that form of prayer which Christ taught his disciples, commonly called the Lord’s Prayer.” (Shorter Catechism Q102)

- God’s ordering of all things (providence): WCF 5.1 — “The Almighty, ... doth uphold, direct, dispose, and govern all creatures, actions, and things, from the greatest even to the least, by his most wise and holy providence, according to his infallible foreknowledge and the free and immutable counsel of his own will, to the praise of the glory of his wisdom, power, justice, goodness and mercy.” (Westminster Confession of Faith, ch. 5.1)

- Assurance that God is able to fulfill his promises (but not a licence to presumption): WCF 14.2 — “By this faith a Christian believeth to be true whatsoever is revealed in the Word, for the authority of God himself speaking therein; and that He is able to do what He hath promised.” (WCF ch. 14.2)

How those standards bear on the Matthew 18:19 practice

- The Standards teach that prayer is to be for things “agreeable to his will” (WSC Q98). That directly qualifies any promise that prayer will “be done” regardless of what is asked. If the request is not agreeable to God’s revealed will or his providence, the Standards do not authorize telling people that God has been “guaranteed” to grant it.

- The Standards also teach God’s sovereign providence over all events (WCF 5.1). Prayer is real and effectual, but it works within God’s infallible counsel and ordering of events. Treating a human formula (two people repeating a precise request verbatim) as a way to override or bind God’s immutable will conflicts with the confession’s teaching about providence.

- The Standards command that prayer follow the Word of God and Christ’s rule (WSC Q102). Matthew 18:19 must be read in the whole Scripture and in its immediate context (see v.20, and the surrounding teaching about church discipline and the Lord’s Prayer as the model). The Standards forbid setting up devotional methods that contradict the Word’s plain rules for prayer and godly humility.

Practical pastoral steps I recommend you take

1) Immediately suspend the “guaranteed” language. Ask the prayer team to stop using spreadsheets or labels that say a request is “guaranteed.” That is theologically and pastorally unsound under the Standards (WSC Q98; WCF 5.1).

2) Teach the prayer team what the Standards require:
   - Read WSC Q98 together and explain: we may and should ask boldly, but we ask “for things agreeable to his will.”

Summary of the relevant standards and how they apply

1) The Fifth Commandment (care and defense of life and family)
- The Catechisms (the Larger and Shorter Catechisms) treat the fifth commandment as requiring the preservation of our own life and the life of others, including a duty to defend persons who are assaulted. That principle implies that Christians may lawfully protect themselves and their children from violent attack, and that a ready defense of persons who are unjustly assaulted is permitted and required as a duty of charity and justice.

How this applies here: a wife who removes herself and her children from immediate danger and uses legal means (police, protective orders) to restrain a violent spouse is acting to preserve life and to defend against assault — not acting in personal vengeance.

2) The duty and role of the civil magistrate
- The Westminster Confession (chapter on the civil magistrate) affirms that the civil magistrate is God’s officer, entrusted with the sword to restrain and punish evil and to protect the innocent and orderly society. Christians are permitted and commanded to make use of civil government for the protection of persons and the punishment of wickedness.

How this applies here: seeking the protection of police, courts, and protective orders is precisely the kind of lawful recourse the Standards expect Christians to use when necessary to restrain evil and secure safety. That is not contrary to Christian forgiveness; it is the right use of lawful means to prevent further harm and to secure justice and peace.

3) Marriage vows and duties
- The Standards teach that marriage is a godly institution ordained for mutual help and comfort within the bounds of God’s law and that married persons have duties to one another. Those duties do not require a spouse to endure ongoing violence or to neglect the welfare of their children.

How this applies here: remaining in a situation where one or one’s children are in danger is not required by any confessionally endorsed notion of marital duty. Protecting the family, seeking safety, and using lawful means to restrain a violent spouse are consistent with the duties of marriage (to protect and care for one another) and with Christian love for the vulnerable.

4) Personal non-retaliation vs. lawful restraint of evil
- The New Testament’s teaching about “turning the other cheek” and against personal vengeance is about Christians not seeking private revenge and about a spirit of meekness and forgiveness. The Westminster Standards distinguish personal non-retaliation and Christian forgiveness from the legitimate role of the magistrate and the legitimate exercise of defense and protection. Those two things are not the same: refusing private vengeance does not require refusing to protect the innocent or refusing to call on lawful authorities.

How this applies here: the pastor rightly differentiated between personal vengeance (which Christians must hate and avoid) and lawful protective measures (which Christians may and should use to preserve life and restrain evil).

- Distinguish pastoral discipline and restoration (which may be appropriate someday if and when there is genuine repentance and changed behavior) from immediate priorities of safety and justice.

Thank you for a clear, serious question. Brief answer up front: do not rush to liquidate or cripple the business out of fear; the Westminster Standards teach that providence, lawful callings, stewardship, and the duty to do good govern how Christians handle wealth. That means you must avoid the love of money, but you are also bound to provide for your family and to use means prudently while giving and doing good. Below I give pastoral counsel and then the specific Westminster texts I am relying on (quoted).

Practical pastoral counsel
- Don’t make a rash, dramatic decision out of fear or guilt. “Sell all” or wholesale liquidation can be an idol of instant holiness if done to show piety rather than out of obedience or wise stewardship.
- Test your motives. The sin named in Scripture and in our tradition is the love of money (not money itself). If your unease is fear of covetousness, confess that and seek help; if it is zeal for holiness, test that zeal by wise counsel and Scripture.
- Provide for your family as a serious Christian duty. The family depends on your provision; deliberate impoverishment that endangers them would be wrong.
- Steward your business and resources: set aside emergency funds, fund obligations, plan charitable giving (regular, sacrificial, and cheerful), and consider setting a generous, concrete plan for giving now and in the future rather than an all-or-nothing act.
- Grow and run the business as a lawful calling for God’s glory and the good of others: lawful industry and prudent saving are not condemned.
- Practice disciplined generosity. Give sacrificially and regularly (a plan helps) so you are not a slave to money, and let your giving be an instrument of grace rather than a way to alleviate conscience alone.
- Seek wise counsel (trustworthy Christian elders / a presbyter or pastor, and your wife, since this affects your household), pray, and act in a way that honors God, protects your family, and does good to others.

Westminster texts relied on (quoted)
- WSC (Shorter Catechism) Q1: “What is the chief end of man? Man’s chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him forever.”
  - How this bears: wealth and callings are to be subordinated to the ultimate end — God’s glory and our enjoyment of him — so money is a means, not an end.

- WCF (Westminster Confession of Faith) 5.1: “God the great Creator of all things doth uphold, direct, dispose, and govern all creatures, actions and things, from the greatest even to the least, by his most wise and holy providence, according to his infallible foreknowledge, and the free and immutable counsel of his own will, to the praise of the glory of his wisdom, power, justice, goodness, and mercy.”
  - How this bears: God governs the distribution of wealth; providence ordinarily works through means (business, inheritance, months of good sales), so your success and the inheritance are providential gifts to be stewarded for his glory.

- WCF 5.5: “God, in his ordinary providence, maketh use of means, yet is free to work without, above, and against them, at his pleasure.”
  - How this bears: It is proper to use means (running and growing your HVAC business, saving for family needs) rather than assume the only faithful posture is to abandon means entirely.

- WCF 16.5 (Of Good Works): “These good works, done in obedience to God’s commandments, are the fruits and evidences of a true and lively faith.” (WCF 16; I quote the clause setting the doctrine that good works flow from faith.)
  - How this bears: Giving, providing for family, honest work, and acts of charity are good works required by God; “sell all” as a proof of piety is not the only good work — faithful provision and charitable use of wealth are also commanded.

A final pastoral word
The Westminster Standards call you to glorify God, to use means faithfully, to do good works, and to live under God’s providence. The teacher you follow is trotting out strong sayings of Scripture out of their contexts; Christ’s commands to the rich are calls against covetousness and to particular discipleship, not a blanket requirement that every Christian must liquidate all. Do not let fear make you reckless; instead, repent where needed, plan generous giving now and ongoing, protect your family, and seek counsel from your church leaders as you form a concrete stewardship plan.

  "God, in his ordinary providence, maketh use of means, yet is free to work without, above, and against them, at his pleasure."

Short answer: No — the Westminster Standards do not teach that believers are “little gods” who can command away sickness by asserting a divine nature. That view conflicts with the Standards’ clear teaching about who God is, who we are, and how God governs the world. Below I give the key texts from the Standards and then practical counsel for your situation.

Key texts (quoted)

- On the one and only living God (God’s unique deity and attributes)
  - WCF 2.1: “There is but one only living and true God, who is infinite in being and perfection, a most pure spirit, invisible, immutable, immense, eternal, incomprehensible, almighty, most wise, most holy, most free, most absolute, working all things according to the counsel of his own immutable and most righteous will, for his own glory; most loving, gracious, merciful, long-suffering, abundant in goodness and truth, forgiving iniquity, transgression and sin; the rewarder of them that diligently seek him; and withal most just and terrible in his judgments, hating all sin, and who will by no means clear the guilty.”

- On the nature of God (shorter catechism)
  - WSC Q4: “What is God? God is a Spirit, infinite, eternal, and unchangeable in his being, wisdom, power, holiness, justice, goodness, and truth.”
  - WSC Q5: “Are there more Gods than one? There is but one only, the living and true God.”

- On God’s providence and secondary causes (how God governs things)
  - WCF 5.1: “God the great Creator of all things, doth uphold, direct, dispose, and govern all creatures, actions, and things, from the greatest even to the least; yet so as thereby neither is God the author of sin, nor is violence offered to the will of the creatures, nor is the liberty or contingency of second causes taken away, but rather established.”

- On the chief end (the Christian’s purpose)
  - WSC Q1: “What is the chief end of man? Man’s chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him forever.”

How these passages bear on the “little gods” / “name it and claim it” teaching

- The Standards repeatedly and unequivocally teach there is one living and true God (WCF 2.1; WSC Q4–5). They do not permit treating creatures (even believers) as little deities. To call Christians “gods” in the sense of possessing the being, attributes, or independent authority of the one God would contradict the confession’s fundamental claim about God’s unique, infinite, and immutable being.

- The Standards also teach that God providentially governs all things (WCF 5.1), while preserving the reality of secondary causes and human responsibility. That means events such as sickness are under God’s sovereign rule, not simply the product of a believer’s failure to “speak” away circumstances. The confession guards against simplistic cause–effect formulas (e.g., “if you do X you will therefore have Y”) and against blaming God for sin. By the same token it does not reduce suffering to merely a faith-deficit in the sufferer or the parent.

- The Christian life’s chief end is to glorify God (WSC Q1). The Standards emphasize trusting Christ, depending on God, prayer, godly means, and submission to God’s will — not claiming an inner divinity to coerce divine action.

Pastoral counsel grounded in the Standards

1. Theologically: The teaching you describe is not taught by the Westminster Standards. The Standards call you to recognize God’s unique deity and to trust his providence. It’s not faithful to say believers are little gods exercising divine power independent of God; rather, Christians are children of God by grace and called to trust and pray to the one living God.

2. Spiritually and pastorally: Do not assume your son’s seizures are necessarily a measure of your spiritual failure. The Standards teach that God governs all things and often works through means. Short answer: No — Jeremiah 29:11 is not a blanket promise that your startup will succeed if you simply “believe big.” The Westminster Standards teach that God governs all things by his providence (and by means), that particular promises must be understood in their scriptural context, and that Christian faith and assurance are not the same as presumptuous or reckless confidence in a particular worldly outcome. Read with that framework, Jer. 29:11 does not justify ignoring prudence, treating your wife harshly, or presuming God has guaranteed the financial outcome you expected.

Key standards I rely on (quoted exactly):

- WCF, Chapter V, Section I:
  "God, the great Creator of all things, doth uphold, direct, dispose, and govern all creatures, actions and things, from the greatest even to the least, by his most wise and holy providence, according to his infallible foreknowledge and the free and immutable counsel of his own will, to the praise of the glory of his wisdom, power, justice, goodness and mercy."

- WCF, Chapter III, Section I:
  "By the decree of God, for the manifestation of his glory, some men and angels are predestinated unto everlasting life, and others foreordained to everlasting death."

- WSC (Shorter Catechism) Question 11 and Answer:
  "Q. 11. What are the works of providence?
   A. The works of providence are God's most holy, wise, and powerful preserving and governing all his creatures, and all their actions."

- WSC Question 1 (to reframe goals and motives):
  "Q. 1. What is the chief end of man?
   A. Man's chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him forever."

How these apply to your situation

1) God governs all things, but he governs through means and according to his counsel — not as a promise that any one plan must succeed. WCF V.1 and WSC Q11 teach that God upholds and governs "all their actions," which includes the ordinary ordering of second causes (business skill, savings, wise counsel). That means trusting God is not the same thing as ignoring means. The Standards reject a view that makes God the author of sin or chaos; he rules providentially, and that providence ordinarily operates through means.

2) God’s eternal decree (WCF III.1) shows that God’s purposes are for his own glory and not merely human prosperity. Predestination doctrine is not a warrant to claim guaranteed material success; the confession frames God's purposes in the scope of his overall glory and mercy, not as an individual promise of wealth or business success.

3) Scripture must be read in context and subordinated to the whole teaching of God’s Word and the church’s doctrine. While the Standards do not comment on Jer. 29:11 line‑by‑line here, they insist that the Scriptures govern faith and life (WCF I generally), and Jer. 29:11 is a promise addressed to exiles with the surrounding command to "seek the peace of the city" (see Jeremiah 29:4–14). It is not a general formula for treating God’s words as a personal ticket to earthly prosperity irrespective of means, counsel, or marital responsibilities.

4) Reorient your motive and end. WSC Q1 reminds us the chief end of man is to glorify God and enjoy him; our projects and plans must be ordered to that end, not personal prestige or proving the "believe big" culture right.

- Humbly hear your wife and trusted, sober counsel. Prudence and "counting the cost" are biblical virtues (and consistent with the Westminster emphasis on means under providence).

Short answer up front: Under the Westminster standards the ritual you describe would be improper and ought not be used if you wish to “honor” a lifelong Presbyterian in a way consistent with her faith. The Confession’s teaching about worship (the regulative principle) and its teaching about liberty of conscience both lead to two conclusions: (1) prayer belongs to God alone and worship practices must be instituted by Scripture, so invoking a departed person to intercede is not an allowable form of worship; (2) family members who conscientiously refuse to participate have a right to abstain and should not be coerced.

Why (briefly, from the Standards)
- The Westminster Confession insists that the acceptable way of worship is instituted by God and set forth in Scripture, and that Christians must not invent new rites or add to God’s appointed worship. That regulative principle (WCF chapter on Religious Worship) rules out privately invented practices presented as worship — especially those that address or invoke the dead.  
- The Standards also teach that prayer is addressed to God; seeking the intercession of the dead is a human invention and, when presented as religious worship, crosses into forbidden superstition or idolatry.  
- At the same time the Confession’s teaching on Christian liberty and conscience says no one should be forced to act against conscience in worship; a faithful elder who refuses to attend is not being merely “rigid,” but acting on conscience under God.

So: your sister is not simply being stubborn. If your mother believed (as a Presbyterian would under the Standards) that prayer to the dead is wrong, then a ritual that asks her “spirit” to intercede would be contrary to her convictions and to the worship God has appointed.

Practical counsel
1. Don’t conduct the proposed petition-burning ritual as part of a memorial that is meant to represent your mother’s faith tradition. It would be both theologically inappropriate from a Westminster/Presbyterian perspective and likely deeply offensive to family and church. It also raises safety and public-order issues (burning things at a portrait is risky and sensational).

2. If you want a multi-faith memorial, be clear and honest about which elements are representative of which traditions. Do not present a ritual that prays to the dead as if it represented Presbyterian belief. If some attendees want to perform personal rituals privately, that’s different — but they should not be presented as part of a memorial “in honor of” your mother’s Presbyterian convictions.

3. Offer alternatives that both honor your mother and avoid the theological problems:
   - Scripture reading (Psalm 23, Psalm 121, John 14, Romans 8:31–39, etc.) and words of thanksgiving to God for her life.  
   - Hymns and congregational singing she loved.  
   - Testimonies and memories from family and friends.  
   - Prayers to God for comfort for the bereaved, thanksgiving for her life, and commendation of her to God’s mercy in Christ (explicitly addressed to God, not to the departed).  
   - A moment of silence for private reflection or writing memories into a memory book (not to be burned or “sent” to her).  
   - A charitable act or memorial gift in her name (serves the living and honors her values).

4. If you want something symbolic: a simple candle of remembrance may be used as a memorial symbol if it is clearly understood as a sign (not an offering to a spirit). But avoid rituals that could be construed as invocation or necromancy.

Responding to the “imposition” objection
- The Standards protect conscience: no one should be forced to take part in worship or practice they judge sinful. So your sister has the right to refuse participation. That is not oppression; it is fidelity to the faith she pledges to uphold.  
- You likewise have liberty to grieve and to express your grief. But Christian liberty is not license to use someone’s religious identity to justify practices that their faith rejects. In a family gathering, the more charitable and faithful course is mutual respect: do not require her to join a practice she believes sinful; likewise do not misrepresent your mother’s faith by insisting that such a ritual “honors” her Presbyterian identity.

How to move forward practically
- Talk to your sister (or the elder-minister) and explain your aims: you want to honor Mom and bring people together. Ask what she would consider a faithful way to honor Mom’s memory. That conversation can avoid escalation and may produce a liturgy that both honors your mother’s convictions and allows others space to grieve.  
- If you want a multi-faith event, structure it so that each tradition is clearly its own segment; make participation voluntary. If you plan anything in the style you described, label it clearly as a private ritual of certain guests (not a Presbyterian memorial), and ideally do it elsewhere and in a way that does not involve evoking the dead or burning objects publicly.  
- If reconciliation is important, consider inviting the church’s minister to lead the memorial service or to offer a pastoral blessing; that will reassure church members and keep the service consistent with your mother’s convictions.

Sample simple outline (consistent with Presbyterian practice)
- Welcome, brief opening Scripture (e.g., Psalm 23).  
- Prayer of thanksgiving to God for her life and testimony (addressed to the triune God).  
- Hymn she loved.  
- Testimonies / brief eulogies.  
- Prayer for the bereaved and commendation of the departed to God’s care in Christ.  
- Silent reflection / a time to write memories into a book.  
- Benediction and dismissal.

Conclusion
Grief is for the living, but honoring someone’s religious commitments means not inventing worship they would have rejected. Your sister’s refusal is defensible from the Westminster standards: prayer to the dead and invented rites are improper, and conscience must be respected. You can still arrange a multi-faith memorial, but do so with clarity, honesty, and alternatives that preserve both the memory of your mother and the conscience of those who loved her. If you want, I can draft a full sample liturgy/text for the memorial that follows the outline above.

One sentence: No — not as written; honor your stewardship of the body, heal the tibia, and change the program so training serves God and health rather than destroying them.

Why, from the Westminster standards (brief): The Westminster Confession and Catechisms teach that our chief end is to glorify and enjoy God, and that Christians are to do good works and live obediently under God’s law. That includes stewardship of the life and health God has given us — not treating the body as an idol to be abused, nor courting self-destruction under the name of “discipline.” Scripture’s commendation of discipline (e.g. “I discipline my body”) is not a warrant for sinful extremes or harming oneself; lawful bodily discipline must be ordered to God’s glory, charity, and the preservation of life.

Practical counsel (short, direct, actionable)
- Immediate: Stop all high‑impact running until a sports‑medicine clinician gives a clear progressive return-to-run plan for this stress fracture. Continuing to run on a tibial stress fracture risks a complete fracture and months lost.
- Medical: Follow the doctor’s guidance for bone healing (often weeks of reduced impact, imaging as needed). If you doubt your doctor, get a second opinion from a sports‑medicine or orthopedic clinician who treats athletes regularly.
- Training alternatives while healing:
  - Replace running with low/zero‑impact conditioning: swimming, aqua jogging, cycling, or an anti‑gravity treadmill as allowed; maintain cardiovascular fitness without loading the tibia.
  - Maintain (and progressively load) strength training for bone and tendon health once allowed: heavy-ish, controlled compound lifts, eccentric work, single‑leg strength as advised.
  - Use progressive return-to-impact protocol: start with walking and brisk walking, then run/walk, increasing load slowly per clinician/PT guidance (avoid “gut it out” mentality).
- Nutrition & recovery:
  - Stop extreme 72‑hour fasts while healing. Long fasts impede recovery and immune/bone repair. If you use fasting for discipline, switch to shorter, controlled fasts or time‑restricted eating that don’t compromise repair.
  - Eat adequate kcal, protein, calcium, vitamin D, and other micronutrients to support bone healing. Prioritize sleep and recovery.
- Volume/intensity: Eliminate doubles and very high daily volumes while recovering; keep intensity controlled even in single sessions. Plan for gradual volume progression (10% rule is a starting heuristic; follow clinical guidance).
- Target reassessment: Sub‑5% bodyfat for a photoshoot is an extreme, potentially dangerous goal for sustained health. Consider a safer, temporary peak (and plan recovery after the shoot). Ask whether the image is worth risking long‑term health and vocation.
- Mental & spiritual care:
  - The feelings T4 describes (training as sole worth, unbearable self‑hatred when missing sessions) are warning signs of idolatry and psychological distress. Seek pastoral counsel and a mental‑health professional experienced with athletes/eating/body‑image issues.
  - Reframe training as a God‑given means for stewardship and service, not as the source of your worth. Confess and repent of any idolizing of performance; pursue Christian community and counseling to heal those deeper issues.

Short answer up front — two truths you need to hold together

- The Westminster teaching: ambition itself is not inherently sinful; our chief end is to glorify God and to use our gifts in lawful industry. But covetousness and envying another’s prosperity are sins (Shorter Catechism Q.1, Q.99–100; WCF on providence and the law). So you must repent of the envy and make your aim Christ‑ward as you pursue wealth lawfully and faithfully.  
- Practically: getting to a personal, realized net worth of $30M in five years from a typical recent‑grad starting point is possible but low probability — it requires choosing extremely high‑risk, high‑reward paths (founder at high‑growth startup, very early equity in a later unicorn, or very exceptional investment returns). Any plan must be honest about the heavy risk, dilution, taxes and plain chance involved.

Below I give (A) short moral/spiritual counsel grounded in the Westminster Standards, then (B) three realistic strategic paths with a concrete 5‑year milestone plan (founder path is the most plausible route to $30M), and (C) immediate next steps you can take this week.

A. Moral and spiritual framing (Westminster standards applied)
- Repent of envy and humiliation. The Tenth Commandment forbids immoderate desire and envying the prosperity of others (Shorter Catechism Q.100). Confess this as sin and ask the Lord for contentment and renewed purpose. This is not “gratitude fluff” — it’s an ethical corrective: envy warps judgment and can make you take sinful shortcuts.  
- Reframe your ambition. The chief end of man is to glorify God and enjoy Him (Shorter Catechism Q.1). Ambition is lawful and even commendable when pursued in a lawful calling, for the common good, and to the glory of God. Set goals that serve neighbor/family and steward God’s gifts.  
- Stewardship and lawful means. The Eighth Commandment forbids unjustly hindering others’ goods (Q.99). Do not pursue wealth by deception, oppression, theft, or harm. Be diligent, honest, and prudent in your calling.  
- Trust Providence. The Westminster Confession teaches God’s providence over all events. Work hard and take risks, but do so with prayer, humility, and reliance on God’s ordering of circumstances.

B. Three strategic paths and a 5‑year plan (milestones by year)
I give three high‑level routes. Pick one primary path and pursue ruthlessly; spreading effort across all three will lower odds of reaching $30M.

Path A — Founder of a high‑growth startup (highest realistic upside)
Why: founding a startup that exits at a high valuation is the clearest route to personal $30M in five years if you retain a meaningful share and the company scales quickly.
Short probability note: low probability, but it’s the path that commonly produces multi‑millions quickly.

Year 0 (months 0–6) — Decide & validate
- Decide market and business model (SaaS, marketplace, AI, vertical tech, biotech with partners). Choose a real, large pain to solve.  
- Build or join a founding team (you should have technologies/cofounder cover gaps). Get MVP/prototype in hands of first customers within 3 months.  
- Milestone: MVP + 3 pilot customers; clear problem/early traction; living frugally; runway of 6–12 months. Personal paper net worth: ~$0–$100k (sweat equity only).

Year 1 — Seed & product–market fit
- Acquire paying customers, demonstrate unit economics, churn < target, CAC:LTV trending right.  
- Raise a seed round ($500k–$2M) if traction is strong (valuation range ~$3–10M).  
- Ownership: as founder you may hold 30–60% after seed (depending on team/structure).  
- Milestone: ARR $200k–$1M; seed raise closed; team of 4–10.

Year 2 — Scale & Series A
- Achieve consistent growth, ARR $1M–5M, solid metrics. Hire sales, engineering, ops.  
- Raise Series A ($5–15M) at valuation $20–80M. Expect dilution; founder ownership may drop to ~15–35% depending.  
- Milestone: ARR >$1M; Series A closed; clear path to large market.

Year 3 — Rapid growth / Series B
- Focus on growth to ARR $10M+ or exponential user growth; expand product and market.  
- Raise Series B ($20–80M) at valuation $80–300M. Founder ownership may be ~5–20% after rounds.  
- Milestone: ARR $10M+; product-market leadership in target vertical.

Year 4 — Late stage scale, strategic partnerships
- Optimize unit economics, prepare for large exit or IPO conversations. Pursue global expansion or profitable scale.  
- Milestone: ARR $30M+ and/or strategic acquisition interest at company valuation $200M–1B.

Year 5 — Exit / liquidity event
- Target exit or IPO. If exit at $300M and your ownership is ~10% → gross proceed ~$30M (before taxes). Smaller exits require larger ownership to net $30M.  
- Milestone: liquidity event. Realized net after taxes could be materially lower.

Key cautions for founder path:
- Dilution, employee equity pools, investor terms, and taxes materially reduce proceeds. Model ownership percentages and expected valuations honestly.  
- Probability is low; you might end up with salary and equity that never converts to $30M. Accept this risk.

Path B — Join an early, extremely fast‑growing startup in a senior early role (equity + salary)
Why: joining as head of engineering/GM with 1–5% at right startup can yield $30M+ if the company becomes a unicorn and you stay till liquidity.
