Preamble — A Christian Covenant of Partnership

We, the undersigned, being believers in the Lord Jesus Christ and members (or regular worshipers) of churches that affirm the Bible as the supreme rule of faith and life, do hereby enter into this covenantal Operating Agreement for [Name of Company], a commercial landscaping partnership, on this ___ day of ______, 20___. We do so before God, and in reliance upon Scripture and the biblical standards of stewardship, justice, charity, truth, and brotherly love (as summarized and applied in the Westminster Standards), that our business may be conducted to the glory of God, the good of our neighbors, and the mutual good of the partners.

We acknowledge that Scripture is our ultimate rule and that the Westminster Confession and Catechisms rightly summarize its teaching concerning lawful callings, stewardship, honest dealing, and the duty of Christians to give and walk in holiness. Acting under that authority, we bind ourselves to the following terms, which we adopt as the practical, moral, and corporate rules that will govern our conduct as partners. We intend these promises to be warm in Christian affection and solemnly binding before God and one another.

Article I — Purpose and Priority
1.1 Purpose. The purpose of our company is to perform commercial landscaping and related services in a manner that honors Christ, serves our clients faithfully, provides honest livelihood for workers, and supports the spread of the gospel.
1.2 Priority of Conscience and Scripture. In any question the partners cannot resolve by mutual agreement, we will seek Scripture-guided counsel and, where needed, submit the matter for decision to the elders of one of our churches or to a Christian arbitration panel chosen under Article IX.

Article II — Reserve Funds (No Interest-bearing Investments)
2.1 Form of Reserve. All company reserve funds (defined as cash retained for operating expenses, contingencies, and foreseeable obligations) shall be held only as tangible cash or in non-interest-bearing safekeeping (for example, a non-interest-bearing business safe-deposit or insured on-site safe), and shall not be placed in any account, bond, investment fund, or other instrument that pays interest, dividends, or other returns.
2.2 Purpose. We adopt this rule because we desire to exercise careful Christian stewardship without making the growth of our reserves a trust in uncertain riches; our hope is in God and not in interest-bearing accumulation.
2.3 Custody and Security. The partners will determine by majority vote the secure manner of holding the cash (safe, safe-deposit box, or equivalent), and will maintain adequate insurance and reasonable safeguards against loss or theft consistent with faithful stewardship.
2.4 Exceptions. Only in case of imminent danger to the business (e.g., theft risk beyond reasonable mitigation) and with unanimous written consent of all partners may the company temporarily deposit reserves in a non-interest-bearing bank account or other secure instrument; such deposit shall be explicitly time-limited and reported to all partners.

Article III — Acquisition of Opportunities in Time of Another’s Need
3.1 Duty of Disclosure. If a partner becomes aware of an opportunity to acquire a competitor’s client list, staff, or other assets cheaply because that competitor or a former partner is in hardship, that partner shall immediately disclose the opportunity in writing to all partners.
3.2 Right of First Offer. Such opportunities belong first to the company. For five (5) business days after disclosure (longer for more complex deals as agreed), the partners shall evaluate the opportunity and decide whether to pursue it as company business.
3.3 Company Pursuit. If a majority of partners vote to pursue the opportunity as company business, the partner who discovered it will co-operate in pursuing it on behalf of the company, and no partner shall personally usurp it or take personal advantage of the information without full disclosure and fair compensation to the company.
3.4 If Declined. If the company, by majority decision, declines to pursue the opportunity within the prescribed period, the partner who disclosed it may pursue it personally only after full disclosure to, and accounting with, the partners for any use of company time, resources, or confidential information. All pursuits must be carried out in accordance with Article VI (no disparagement).

Article IV — Honest Books; Contracts and Payment
4.1 Accurate Records. Each partner shall ensure that company books are honest, accurate, and maintained according to customary and reasonable accounting methods. Records shall include receipts, invoices, payroll, and entries adequate to show true financial condition.
4.2 Open Access. Company records shall be open at reasonable times to inspection by any partner. A partner seeking inspection shall not be unreasonably denied and shall be given copies of documents reasonably requested.
4.3 Timely Payment. The company shall render to every subcontractor, supplier, and worker exactly what our contract or agreement with them specifies, and shall pay promptly according to the agreed terms. No partner shall divert funds owed to a subcontractor or supplier for personal use.
4.4 Annual Review/Audit. The partners shall cause an annual financial review (internal or by an independent Christian bookkeeper/accountant as agreed) and report the results openly to all partners.

Article V — Partner Compensation; Test of Hearts
5.1 Base Compensation Rule. No partner shall receive a salary or draw from the company at a rate higher than the hourly wage or equivalent annualized pay of the lowest-paid field crew member employed by the company at that time.
5.2 Increase Procedure and Test. A partner seeking a higher salary must:
  (a) Present in writing the reason for the requested increase to the partners;
  (b) Spend thirty (30) consecutive days living on the crew wage (recorded and verifiable by receipts and testimony) and during that month participate in field work as scheduled, so that his or her walk and heart are tested in sympathy with lower-paid workers; and
  (c) After completion, present a written account of the month and evidence of living on the wage.
5.3 Approval. After completion of the test in 5.2, an increase may be approved only by unanimous consent of the other partners. If the other partners withhold approval, the requesting partner remains entitled only to the base compensation in 5.1.
5.4 Temporary Relief. Nothing in this Article prevents partners from receiving temporary reimbursements for documented, necessary business expenses or from receiving occasional bonuses approved unanimously by the partners.

Article VI — Gospel-first Profit Share and Giving
6.1 First Fruits. Before any partner draws profit distributions, the company shall set aside and pay a fixed share of net annual profit to gospel work. The partners agree that this fixed share shall be ten percent (10%) of net profit (or such other percentage as the partners may unanimously amend in writing).
6.2 Designation of Recipients. The recipients of this gospel share shall be approved by unanimous consent of the partners and shall be Christian ministries or churches whose primary purpose is the clear preaching and teaching of the gospel. The partners may rotate or vary recipients by unanimous agreement.
6.3 Timing. The gospel share shall be distributed within thirty (30) days following the annual accounting for the year, before partners draw any profit distributions.
6.4 Record of Giving. All such charitable distributions shall be recorded in the company books and available for inspection.

Article VII — No Disparagement; Honest Competition
7.1 No Badmouthing. No partner shall disparage, slander, or make misleading statements about a current competitor or a former partner for the purpose of gaining bids, clients, or any advantage. Advertising and solicitation shall be honest, accurate, and fair.
7.2 Communication. If a partner believes a competitor or former partner has acted wrongly or unlawfully, the partner shall not use that belief to slander for gain; rather, concerns shall be pursued through lawful channels or submitted to the partners for company response.
7.3 Remedy. A partner who violates this Article shall be required to make public retraction and apology acceptable to the partners and, where harm has occurred, to make restitution and accept discipline under Article VIII.

Article VIII — Discipline, Restitution, and Removal
8.1 Pastoral Admonition First. When a partner breaches any substantial provision of this Agreement, the partners shall first pursue restoration and correction in the spirit of Matthew 18:15–17: private admonition, then with witnesses if needed, then before the company.
8.2 Restitution. A partner who has caused loss or harm to the company or to a third party through willful breach must make full restitution as far as possible, in addition to any company discipline.
8.3 Suspension and Removal. For persistent, willful, or gross breaches (including misuse of company funds, deliberate fraud, repeated violation of Articles II–VII, or refusal to submit to restoration), the partners may, by unanimous vote of the others (excluding the partner in question), suspend that partner’s right to compensation and drawing privileges and may remove the partner from the company. Removal shall require an offer of fair buyout terms for the departing partner’s interest, or, failing agreement, binding appraisal and purchase under the arbitration procedures of Article IX.
8.4 Restoration. If the removed partner repents and shows credible evidence of restoration, the partners may, at their discretion, restore some or all former privileges consistent with justice and prudence.

Article IX — Dispute Resolution and Church Ordained Arbitration
9.1 Brotherly Resolution. The partners commit to seek to resolve disputes openly, patiently, and in Christian charity.
9.2 Arbitration. If the partners cannot resolve a dispute among themselves within thirty (30) days, they shall submit the dispute to binding Christian arbitration. The arbitration panel shall consist of two elders (or mature elders’ representatives) from churches of two different partners, together with an agreed neutral Christian businessperson experienced in commercial matters. The panel’s decision shall be final and binding on the partners.
9.3 Procedure. Arbitration shall follow agreed rules of fairness, allow full presentation of evidence, and require written findings and orders, including, if appropriate, restitution, buyout amounts, or other equitable remedies.

Article X — Amendment, Duration, and Final Oath
10.1 Amendment. This Agreement may be amended only by unanimous written consent of all partners and only after prayerful consideration, reading of amendments aloud, and, where practical, counsel from an elder or Christian counselor. No amendment shall lessen a partner’s duty of honest dealing or the gospel-first giving required in Article VI without unanimous consent.
10.2 Duration. This covenant shall endure for so long as the company exists. If the company is dissolved, any remaining cash and assets after debts are paid shall first satisfy Article VI’s gospel-first share for that year and then be distributed among partners according to agreed ownership percentages.
10.3 Final Oath. We enter into this Agreement in the presence of the living God and bind ourselves to it conscientiously. We pledge to one another to seek holiness and repentance when we fail, to apply biblical church discipline when needed, and to labor diligently for the glory of Christ in this common calling.

Short answer: by the Westminster Standards the second elder is right. The Standards do not permit the Session to bind uncommanded “holy days” on the consciences of the people as required worship. You may teach about and recommend historic seasons as helpful devotional aids, and you may hold voluntary services around them, but you may not make them obligatory worship or impose them under church authority.

Why (Confessional reasoning, briefly)
- The Confession teaches the Regulative Principle of worship — the way and elements of acceptable worship must be instituted by God in Scripture. Worship which is not instituted by God in His Word must not be required of the conscience. (See WCF on Religious Worship; cf. Larger/Shorter Catechisms on worship and the Lord’s Day.)
- The Confession also insists “God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men which are in anything contrary to his Word, or beside it, in matters of faith and worship.” (WCF ch. 20) That rules out imposing rites or festivals not commanded in Scripture.
- The Confession recognizes the Lord’s Day as the Christian Sabbath to be kept holy; it does not identify Advent, Lent, Ash Wednesday, Maundy Thursday, or commemorations of saints as required Christian holy days. The only ordinary national “days” the civil magistrate may lawfully call are extraordinary fasts or thanksgivings (as provided by the Confession/Directory), not permanent new church holy days imposed by a Session.

Pastoral/practical ruling you can give the congregation
1. Ruling (short, firm)
   - The Session finds that we may not impose historically extra‑biblical holy days or seasons as required elements of corporate worship. Participation in observances such as Advent, Lent, Ash Wednesday imposition of ashes, Maundy Thursday, or saints’ commemoration shall be voluntary and not required for membership, reception to the Lord’s Supper, discipline, or any other ecclesiastical sanction.

2. What the Session will permit and encourage
   - The Session will allow instruction about the historic church year and may offer teaching series and voluntary worship services during these seasons as pastoral helps for spiritual growth.
   - Such services must conform to the Regulative Principle (only those elements of public worship which Scripture prescribes or approves), must not present these observances as necessary to salvation, and must not require participation.
   - The Session will avoid rites or language that presume sacramental or quasi‑sacramental efficacy for practices not instituted in Scripture (for example, treating ashes as having saving or purifying power), and will avoid any form of saint veneration that attributes mediatorial or salvific functions to the departed.

3. If members wish to observe privately
   - Members are free in conscience to keep devotional seasons privately or with one another, provided this is not enforced by the Session and provided their practice does not contradict Scripture.

4. If you want more definite text to use
   - Announce to the congregation: “The Session recognizes the devotional value some find in the historic church seasons. We will teach and offer optional services but will not make these observances church requirements. The Lord’s Day remains the established Christian day of public worship, and extraordinary fasts/thanksgivings remain matters for civil or corporate appointment as the Confession describes.”

If you expect further controversy
- Point people to the Confession’s teaching (Regulative Principle; WCF ch. 20 on conscience; WCF ch. 21 on worship and the Lord’s Day) and to the Directory for Public Worship for historical guidance. Seek to educate the congregation about why confessional Presbyterians have historically resisted imposed holy‑day observance while also practicing pastoral charity toward those who find spiritual profit in certain liturgical seasons — provided those practices remain voluntary.

Team Culture & Conduct Code — [Team Name]
Preamble
We are a co‑ed community youth team coached in the spirit of service, discipline, and mutual respect. We operate to give each player opportunity to grow in skill, character, and teamwork. The following Code balances safety, fairness, and the Christian virtues of love, justice, humility, and stewardship. Compliance is required for participation.

1) Core Expectations (binding)
- Attendance & Punctuality: Players arrive ready to begin at the posted time. Repeated lateness may affect playing time per the coach’s discretion (see section 6).
- Respect for Officials & Opponents: All players must treat referees, opponents, and volunteers with courtesy. Abusive language or gestures toward referees, opponents, or volunteers will be disciplined.
- Team Uniform & Appropriate Athletic Attire: Players must wear the league uniform for games. Practice attire must be safe and appropriate for play (no jewelry that creates safety hazards; soccer-appropriate tops, shorts/leggings or athletic pants). The coach reserves the right to require clothing that does not create a safety issue or unfair advantage.
- Supervised Transport & Safety: All transport arrangements must be logged with the coach and approved by parents/guardians. The team requires that any youth driver meet league/insurance requirements and have written parental permission. The coach will not leave a player unsupervised; rides home must be with an approved adult or with parent permission.
- Communication: Parents and players should raise concerns privately with the coach first. Campaigning through public team chats, pressure campaigns, or attempts to influence team decisions via public pressure will not be tolerated. Repeated public campaigning may result in restricted access to team channels.
- Non‑discrimination & Dignity: No player will be shamed, penalized, or benched for reasons of family finances, clothing being a hand‑me‑down, race, sex, religion, or other protected characteristic. We will support players who need assistance to meet uniform/gear standards.

2) Music and Practice Atmosphere
- The coach will control music used at practice. To maintain a focus on instruction, safety, and an inclusive environment, music played at practice must be clean, non‑explicit, and chosen by the coach or by team consensus under coach supervision. If families wish to provide a playlist for voluntary bus rides or optional team gatherings, that must be approved in advance by the coach.

3) Modesty & Attire Standards
- We require athletic clothing appropriate to the sport. Modesty expectations are applied equally to all players, male and female, and are intended for safety and dignity. The coach will provide specific guidance (e.g., no excessively revealing tops, shorts of sufficient length for safe play), but will not impose gender‑targeted restrictions that treat girls differently than boys for the same activity.

4) Conduct, Bullying & Discipline
- Bullying, harassment, or exclusionary behavior will not be tolerated. Consequences are progressive: verbal warning → parent conference → temporary suspension → removal from the roster for repeated or serious infractions.
- Discipline decisions will be documented. Players and parents may appeal disciplinary action to the team committee within 7 days.

5) Playing Time & Leadership Positions
- Playing time and captaincy are coaching decisions based on transparent criteria: attendance, attitude, effort, coachability, teamwork, and demonstrated skill in training and games.
- There will be no guarantees, quotas, or secret arrangements to favor particular players because of parental influence, donations, or external pressure. “Rewarding commitment” may be recognized by built‑in incentives (extra leadership responsibilities, transparent merit‑based recognition), but not by behind‑the‑scenes preferential playing time or secret arrangements.

6) New Players & Financial Hardship
- Players who lack matching gear or who have hand‑me‑down uniforms will not be shamed, docked, or benched for that reason. Families needing assistance will be referred confidentially to the team fundraising/assistance process. Coaches will accommodate reasonable substitutions so every player can participate.

7) Faith & Voluntary Religious Activities
- The team respects the religious convictions of families. The coach will not require players to sign religious pledges as a condition of participation.
- Voluntary, opt‑in faith activities (e.g., optional pre- or post‑practice prayers, Bible study, or devotional gatherings) may be organized by parents or players outside of official practice/game time; participation is strictly voluntary and no one will be pressured or penalized for non‑participation. Team‑organized devotional activities will be open and clearly labeled as voluntary.

8) Parents’ Role & Communication Protocol
- Discuss concerns with the coach first. If unresolved, the next step is a private meeting with the coach and, if necessary, a member of the team committee.
- Public campaigning, widespread messaging, or attempts to coerce coaches through social media or team chat are disruptive and contrary to team health; this behavior may result in restricted participation in team communications.

9) Enforcement & Appeals
- The coach and team committee will enforce this code consistently and document decisions. Appeals go to the team committee; serious disputes may be escalated to league leadership.

Acceptance
Both player and at least one parent/guardian must sign to acknowledge receipt, acceptance of the Code, and willingness to abide by it while on the roster.

What I will keep from the loudest parents’ demands
- I keep: A clear expectation of respectful behavior, modest/appropriate athletic attire, supervised transport, and a sober, focused practice environment without offensive or explicit music. These promote safety, dignity, and team discipline.
- I keep: The league’s existing rules on respectful language, appropriate athletic attire, and supervised transport — we will not strip them out. (Those are baseline safety and sportsmanship rules.)

What I will not put in (and why)
- I will not require a mandatory religious “purity pledge” as a condition of team membership. Reason: making a religious pledge a condition of participation compels conscience and risks excluding or coercing players and families of different convictions. The Westminster Confession (Ch. 20) affirms that God alone is Lord of the conscience; the coach must avoid compelling religious acts in a public/community team setting. Voluntary faith opportunities are permitted, but they cannot be prerequisite for participation.
- I will not impose gender‑specific dress rules that single out girls (e.g., “only knee‑length shorts for the girls” but not boys). Reason: fairness, safety, and uniform application of modesty standards require equal treatment. Differential rules target a protected class and risk shaming.
- I will not bar mixed‑gender carpools categorically. Reason: logistical and safety realities make neutral, supervised carpools necessary. Instead I require parental approval and documented arrangements; the priority is safe, supervised transport, not a blanket ban.
- I will not include any hidden clause that steers playing time or captaincy to particular players because of their family’s influence or donations. Reason: fairness, integrity, and trust require transparent, merit‑based selection. Secret arrangements violate the team covenant and harm the group.

How the Westminster Standards inform these decisions (brief)
- Christian liberty and conscience: WCF Chapter 20 teaches that God alone is Lord of the conscience; human authorities should not compel religious practices in matters that are not essential. This supports offering voluntary faith activities rather than coercive pledges.
- Duty of love, justice, and equity: The Standards emphasize charity and justice — we must treat every player fairly and avoid favoritism.
- Order and discipline: The Standards also approve orderly governance and discipline in assemblies (e.g., the church). That supports having a clear, binding code and fair enforcement.

Final note from the coach
I want this team to be a place where players grow athletically, socially, and in character. I will enforce the Code consistently and transparently. I invite parents to sign the Code, support the coach’s decisions, and bring concerns privately so we can resolve them quickly. Where conscience or faith practices are involved, I will protect individual liberty and make devotional participation purely voluntary.

Preamble — Purpose and Authority
We are a small discipleship household, formed to live together under Christ’s Lordship, to stir one another to love and good works, and to be formed in holiness by word, sacrament, prayer, work, and mutual accountability. This Rule of Life is a covenant: a warm but binding agreement among the residents and the house leaders (hereafter “the Leaders”) intended to promote spiritual growth, gospel fellowship, and freedom from covetousness and worldly anxiety.

This covenant is grounded in the biblical duty of Christians to pursue godliness, to practice mutual watchfulness and churchly discipline, and to labor for the good of the household and the church. In keeping with the principles of the Westminster Standards concerning the care and correction of God’s people, we submit to mutually agreed boundaries so our lives and resources are ordered to the glory of God and the good of our brothers and sisters.

Commitment
By signing below each resident voluntarily enters this covenant for the agreed term (initial term: 6 months, renewable) and agrees to be held accountable to the Leaders and to the processes stated here. Residents retain the right to withdraw from the house at any time; the Leaders will not coerce or unlawfully impede departure. Where discipline is needed, it will be administered with pastoral care and opportunity for repentance and restoration.

Articles of the House Rule of Life
1. Worship and Gathering
- Each resident commits to attend the house’s Sunday gathering and the midweek (Wednesday) gathering unless prevented by legitimate and communicated cause (work, illness, urgent necessity). Repeated unexcused absence will be addressed by the Leaders in the spirit of restoration.

2. Stewardship and a Monthly Financial Cap
- The Leaders will set a monthly cap on individual earnings, savings accumulation, and spending that applies to all residents. The cap is intended to foster contentment and dependence upon God rather than the pursuit of more: “the contented heart doesn’t need more.”
- No resident may intentionally earn, save beyond, or spend beyond the cap without prior approval from the Leaders. Pursuing a raise, side income, or any new income-generating activity requires written approval from the Leaders in advance. Requests will be considered in light of spiritual maturity, household needs, and the resident’s vocation and responsibilities.
- Emergency expenditures (medical emergencies, legal obligations, sudden family crisis) that cannot be covered by the cap are exempted; in such cases the resident will notify a Leader as soon as reasonably possible and document the need.

3. Transparency and Shared Stewardship
- The house maintains a shared budget spreadsheet that is visible to all housemates. Each resident agrees to keep their relevant budget entries up to date and honest.
- Any single purchase of more than $40 for personal or household use shall be posted to the house communication channel with amount, purpose, and a brief explanation, so the community may weigh in. This practice is to nurture mutual accountability and to “kill covetousness in community.”
- All residents agree to contribute to a common meal fund (amount and method of contribution set by the Leaders) and to participate in the decision-making about common expenditures.

4. Chores, Common Life, and Contribution
- Residents will contribute their fair share to household chores, maintenance, and community responsibilities as scheduled by the house. Persistent failure to carry out agreed duties will be addressed by the Leaders and may result in corrective measures.

5. Employment and Relocation
- Residents may not accept an employment offer that would require moving to another city without first seeking and receiving a formal release from the Leaders. The Leaders’ release will be granted only after pastoral conversation concerning motive, the resident’s spiritual welfare, and the wellbeing of the household. (We recognize that discontentment can masquerade as opportunity; this rule is intended to ensure discernment.)
- The Leaders will make every effort not to unreasonably withhold a release; appeals are possible (see Discipline & Appeals).

Discipline, Correction, and Consequences
- The aim of correction is repentance, restoration, and the glory of Christ (Galatians 6:1; Matthew 18:15–20). Discipline will be graduated and pastoral:
  1. Private conversation and admonition from a Leader.
  2. Formal meeting with Leaders and written expectations (restoration plan).
  3. Probationary status with specific conditions and a set review date.
  4. If unrepentant or if covenant breach is repeated or serious, the Leaders may require the resident to leave the house. Requiring a resident to leave is a last resort undertaken after prayerful attempts at restoration.
- For breaches involving dishonesty, financial malfeasance, or abuse of others, Leaders retain the right to immediate protective action (including suspension from house privileges or immediate removal) while investigations proceed.

Leaders’ Responsibilities and Accountability
- The Leaders covenant to shepherd the household with humility, transparency, and love. Leaders will:
  - Apply the Rule consistently and fairly.
  - Maintain the shared budget spreadsheet and provide periodic reports.
  - Review the monthly cap at least quarterly and communicate rationale for any change.
  - Submit to oversight by our sponsoring church/elder body (or an agreed external accountability body). Residents may bring grievances to that body if needed.
  - Not withhold release unreasonably; if denial occurs, Leaders will provide written reasons and a pathway for appeal.

Amendments, Review, and Term
- This Rule of Life is to be reviewed at minimum every three months by Leaders with resident input. Amendments may be made by Leaders with the assent of a majority of residents, provided core spiritual commitments remain.
- Initial covenant term is six months. Renewal is explicit; nothing in this covenant creates involuntary servitude. Residents may leave at will; Leaders will provide reasonable assistance for departure logistics when a resident is asked to leave.

Signatures
By signing below I acknowledge I have read, understood, and willingly enter this covenant as written. I affirm that I am entering voluntarily and that I am free to depart the household at any time. I also acknowledge the Leaders’ responsibility to shepherd, correct, and, if necessary, remove for the health of the household.

Sacred Arts Policy
(Adopted under Session authority — for the arts ministry of [Church Name], a congregation subscribing to the Westminster Standards)

Prefatory statement
We rejoice that the Triune God is the giver of beauty and that the Gospel renews all life, including our use of the arts. At the same time we are a confessional, Presbyterian church and therefore order our worship and the use of images and ornament according to Scripture and the Westminster Standards (which apply the regulative principle of worship and the teaching of the second commandment). This policy states how we will welcome, commission, display, and use visual art in our buildings and services in a way that is pastorally wise, theologically faithful, and practically clear.

Foundational principles (short)
- Scripture and the Westminster Standards govern: worship must be conducted according to God’s revealed will; nothing is to be employed in worship as though instituted by Christ unless Scripture authorizes it.
- The second commandment forbids making or using images as objects of religious worship or as aids that become means of grace or substitutes for Christ. Images used in non‑worship contexts for instruction, decoration, or memory are not thereby forbidden by the Standards, provided they are not presented as aids to salvation or worship.
- Distinction: “in worship” (elements instituted by Christ and presented as means of grace) versus “in church life” (instruction, decoration, children’s teaching, historical display, and so on). The former calls for special caution and Session oversight; the latter may be allowed with pastoral prudence.
- Session oversight: The Session has the final authority to approve any visual element used in the gathered public worship of the congregation.

Policy and rulings (binding)

1) Large realistic painted portrait of Jesus hung over the communion table
Ruling: Not permitted.
Rationale: The Westminster Standards require that no image of God be used as an object or focal point of worship. To hang a realistic portrait of the incarnate Lord immediately over the Lord’s Table and to present it as the congregation’s worshipful focus would function as an image of devotion and risk idolatry or the confusion of means. Accordingly, no image purporting to be “the Son’s actual face” shall be placed above, behind, or otherwise as the centerpiece of the communion table or presented in the gathered Lord’s Supper as a focus, aid to grace, or object of prayer.
Pastoral alternative: The donor is warmly invited to offer the painting for non‑sanctuary display (e.g., a foyer gallery or a classroom), clearly labeled as an artistic representation and not as a focus for worship, or to consider a commissioned abstract or symbolic work (e.g., cross motif, scriptural text, or other non‑figurative piece) that the Session may accept for placement in the sanctuary if that is judged appropriate.

2) Total ban on all visual art in the building (no images at all)
Ruling: Not adopted.
Rationale: While the Standards firmly condemn images used superstitiously or as means of grace, they do not require the elimination of all visual art from church property. A strict, across‑the‑board ban on every likeness (photographs, architectural ornament, children’s books, banners, etc.) is an interpretive extreme not required by the Westminster Standards. The Session therefore will not impose a blanket prohibition on all visual art. However, the use and placement of any visual element will be governed by the principles below and by Session approval when used in public worship.
Practical limit: Visual elements that are likely to be prayed to, venerated, or presented as having salvific or sacramental efficacy will be refused. Decorative or instructional uses that are clearly non‑worshipful and do not claim mediatorial power may be permitted with pastoral oversight.

3) Children’s illustrated Bible storybooks and flannelgraph showing simple drawn figures, including Jesus and the disciples, in children’s ministry
Ruling: Permitted, with guidelines.
Rationale: The Westminster Standards allow for faithful, non‑superstitious instruction. For the formation of young children, simple pictorial aids that tell biblical stories are a legitimate pedagogical tool. These items are permitted in the church’s children’s ministry provided they are used as teaching aids — not as objects of devotion or as substitutes for catechesis grounded in Scripture. Such depictions must not be presented as the literal, definitive “face of Jesus” nor employed in worship services as an object to be bowed before or prayed to.
Guidelines: Materials chosen should be age‑appropriate, theologically sound, and competent in representing biblical truth. Leaders will explain to children (in age‑appropriate language) that pictures are human attempts to illustrate biblical truth, not objects of worship. The arts ministry will maintain an approved list of children’s visual resources consistent with these guidelines.

4) Projection of abstract, non‑figurative imagery (light, color, moving texture) behind congregational singing
Ruling: Conditionally permitted for use during gathered singing, subject to Session approval and the “no means of grace” rule.
Rationale: Abstract, non‑figurative imagery does not depict God or Christ and so avoids the particular dangers of picturing the Godhead. The regulative principle cautions us about creating novel “elements” of worship, but it does not forbid pastoral aids or environmental lighting when they are clearly incidental, subordinate to the Word, and not presented as sacramental or revelatory. Therefore the Session may authorize the projection of abstract imagery as an atmospheric aid during singing so long as it is (a) clearly decorative/ambient, (b) not presented to the congregation as a means of grace or as mediating revelation, and (c) under the session’s direction as to content, timing, and appropriateness.
Operational requirements: Proposals must state the purpose, samples of imagery, technical controls (to avoid distracting movement), and assurances that the imagery is non‑figurative and non‑ritualized. The Arts Ministry will keep projected imagery conservative and subordinate to Scripture and corporate worship.

5) Framed printed Scripture text and the church’s historic confession in the entryway
Ruling: Permitted and encouraged.
Rationale: Posting Scripture and our confession as texts for reading, catechesis, and witness is consistent with the Standards’ stress upon the Word and confessional subscription. Such framed texts in common areas do not constitute images of the divine and serve the church’s instructive and pastoral purposes.
Format expectations: Texts should be displayed reverently, accompanied by explanatory captions if helpful, and curated by the Arts Ministry and Session.

6) Any visual element used in the gathered public service
Ruling: Must be approved by Session and must never be presented as a means of grace.
Rationale: In keeping with the regulative principle and our confessional commitments, anything used in the public worship service must have Session approval. No visual element may be presented as if it confers or mediates grace (i.e., as a sacramental substitute, a symbol that is treated as efficacious apart from God’s institution, or a channel of special revelation).
Approval process: The Arts Ministry will submit a written description (purpose, images or samples, timing in the service, technical requirements, and pastoral rationale) to the Session at least two weeks prior to the proposed use. Emergency exceptions must be approved by the Pastor and Moderator of Session.

Other operating norms (brief)
- Location matters: Visuals used in worship spaces (sanctuary) are treated with greater caution than those used in hallways, classrooms, or the foyer.
- Labels and explanations: When a visual could be misunderstood, a brief explanatory label or printed note shall accompany it (e.g., “artistic representation — not an object of worship”).
- Donor gifts: Gifts of art may be accepted subject to these rules. Donors will be informed in writing of the Session’s right to place, move, or decline display.
- Review and appeal: The Session will review this policy at least every three years. Concerns may be brought to the Session in writing and will be considered in light of Scripture, the Westminster Standards, and pastoral care.

Closing pastoral note
We desire art that points us to the glory of Christ without substituting human images for the living God. We welcome faithful creativity that serves the proclamation of the Word, the nurture of our children, and the life of the congregation — ever under the oversight of the Session and the conviction of Scripture and our confessional standards.

Worship Renewal Covenant of [Church Name]

Preamble
We, the members of [Church Name], acknowledging our need of renewing grace and desiring to worship God acceptably and in purity, adopt this Worship Renewal Covenant. We do so to encourage reverent, edifying, and orderly services; to provide for faithful pastoral ministry and mutual care; and to protect the consciences and persons of all who worship with us. This Covenant is adopted by the Session as an order of worship and a guide for pastoral oversight, and it is to be administered in accordance with Holy Scripture and the Westminster Confession of Faith (ch. 21, 30) and our church’s rules for discipline.

Article I — Time, Order, and Duration
1. Sunday public worship shall begin at 10:00 a.m. sharp. Members and regular attendees are asked to be present and seated by that time.
2. Each service shall follow a printed order of worship prepared by the pastors and approved by the Session. The printed order shall be made available to the congregation.
3. Services will ordinarily run about ninety (90) minutes. Pastors and leaders will seek to keep services within that frame except for reasonable variations for special services.

Article II — A Time of Pastoral Activation (Prayerful Impartation)
1. The Session authorizes a designated portion of the service (hereafter called the “Activation”) for pastoral prayer, brief spoken encouragement, and the offering of timely, tested ministry words intended for the edification of the congregation.
2. The Session teaches that saving and sanctifying grace comes from God through His Word, sacraments, prayer, and the ordinary means of grace appointed by Christ (WCF ch. 21). The Activation is a permitted and pastoral means of mutual encouragement and prayer, not a novel or exclusive channel of grace, and the service is not made incomplete in Scripture by absence of any single human action.
3. All spoken “words” in Activation shall be the responsibility of the appointed leader(s). Such words must be sober, brief, and subject to pastoral and elder oversight. The elders shall provide means to test, review, and correct anything said publicly in Activation that is questionable, misleading, or sinful.

Article III — Laying on of Hands and Voluntary Reception
1. The laying on of hands by ordained leaders for prayer is a permitted act of pastoral care and prayer (cf. Acts, epistles). It may be used during Activation or other approved times.
2. Receiving such prayer by physical gesture is wholly voluntary. No member or attendee shall be required to adopt any physical posture (e.g., falling backward, prostration). Members shall not be shamed, disciplined, or recorded for failing to perform any particular bodily response.
3. If a member consistently declines offered pastoral prayer in ways that suggest unresolved conflict with the elders or the people of God, elders shall pursue gentle private pastoral conversation to determine pastoral needs and to offer counsel and reconciliation in love (WCF ch. 30). Such private pastoral follow-up is pastoral care, not punitive recordation as “resistance.”
4. Any use of physical gesture that risks injury, coercion, or manipulation is forbidden in our services.

Article IV — Music and Singing
1. Sung praise in public worship shall be drawn from the congregation’s approved psalter-and-hymn list as kept by the Session.
2. The Session will maintain and make available the approved list and the principles by which materials are approved, consistent with the doctrines and piety of the church.

Article V — Monthly Members’ Meeting and Confession
1. The congregation shall hold a monthly members’ meeting for purposes of instruction, mutual exhortation, and the orderly exercise of church discipline as Scripture and the Westminster Standards require.
2. The Session encourages members personally to confess sin to God and, when appropriate, to one another (cf. James 5:16, Matt. 5:23–24). The monthly members’ meeting shall include times of corporate confession and mutual prayer; however, no member shall be required publicly to name private sins of heart (for example, specific jealous feelings) unless under legitimate church discipline for a public offense or impenitent scandal.
3. If a member acknowledges jealousy, bitterness, or other sin that affects others or the peace of the church, the Session may, in pastoral prudence, invite the person to private confession, counsel, and reconciliation. Where discipline is required for unrepentant sin, the Session shall follow the procedures of church discipline set out in Scripture and WCF ch. 30.

Article VI — Discipline, Testing, and Safeguards
1. Speech or actions in worship that claim special revelation contrary to Scripture, that manipulate or coerce, or that cause scandal shall be tested and, if necessary, corrected or prohibited by the Session.
2. Elders are charged to exercise oversight humbly and lovingly. Any complaint about Activation words, pastoral behavior, or member conduct shall be brought to the Session for careful and Scriptural examination.
3. The Session shall keep a confidential process for review of Activation ministry and for appeals, seeking the peace of the church and the restoration of the sinner.

Article VII — Adoption, Amendment, and Binding Force
1. This Covenant is adopted by the Session on [date] and shall be binding as a pastoral and liturgical order of this congregation. It is to be administered in conformity with Holy Scripture and the Westminster Standards.
2. Amendments to this Covenant require the recommendation of the Session and the concurrence of a stated members’ meeting called for that purpose.
3. Nothing in this Covenant shall require action or posture that would violate a member’s conscience or the clear teaching of Holy Scripture as summarized in the Westminster Standards.

Short answer up front

- On streaming the service: The Westminster Standards do not require tearing out cameras or screens. Audio/video equipment used to extend the ordinary means of worship to those who cannot be present is a lawful use of indifferent (adiaphorous) means so long as it is governed by the Word of God and ordered to the glory of God. The elder therefore may not lawfully forbid a lawful means of worship simply because it is “worldly.” The session, however, does have authority to regulate how those means are used so that worship remains reverent and biblical.

- On a “virtual Lord’s Supper” (people at home using their own elements while the minister speaks over a camera): This departs from the form and administration of the sacrament as set down in Scripture and the Standards. The Lord’s Supper is a sacrament instituted to be administered by the church’s officers according to Christ’s appointment; it is not rightly conveyed by anonymous, self-served participation remote from the minister and visible congregation. The pastor should not authorize remote self-communion as a valid administration of the sacrament.

Grounding in the Standards (principles and application)

1) Principles that govern both questions
- Worship and sacraments are to be “regulated by the Word of God.” (WCF: the public worship of God is to be ordered by Scripture.) Practices that are plainly instituted in Scripture must be observed; practices that are not instituted must not be added as parts of worship.
- At the same time, the Standards recognize Christian liberty about things indifferent (adiaphora): God alone is Lord of the conscience; the church may use lawful things not expressly forbidden by Scripture if they help the worship of God and are used in subjection to His Word.
- The church’s officers have authority to order and govern public worship and the administration of the sacraments, but that authority is bounded: they must not command or forbid what Scripture allows or require what Scripture does not require.

2) Streaming the service (cameras/screens)
- Why streaming is lawful: A camera, microphone, projector, livestream, etc., are means — not a new element of worship. They are tools used to convey the ordinary, Scriptural elements of worship (reading, preaching, prayer, singing, sacraments) to those who for legitimate reasons cannot be physically present. Under the Standards such means are adiaphora: lawful when used to the glory of God and under the Word.
- The elder’s proposal to “tear it all out” treats an indifferent means as if it were a prohibited element. That would be an unlawful forbidding of a lawful thing. The session should not do that.
- Session responsibility: The session may and should regulate the use of technology so worship is reverent and scripturally ordered (camera placement, who operates, when screens are used, no distracting on-screen overlays, no liturgical innovations via media). If the elder’s concern is holiness and reverence, address the concern by regulation and discipline of practice rather than by wholesale prohibition.
- Practical pastoral steps: Keep streaming for shut-ins and those genuinely prevented from attending. Limit interactivity (no live chat affecting the service), limit visual intrusion into the worship space, adopt policies for when/where cameras and screens are used, and periodically review with the session.

3) The “virtual Lord’s Supper”
- What the Standards require: The Lord’s Supper is a sacrament instituted by Christ to be administered to the visible church as a sign and seal of the covenant. The outward elements (bread and wine) are to be used according to Christ’s institution, and sacraments are ordinarily to be administered by those who are appointed to that task (the officers of the church) and in the visible assembly of the church under the Word.
- Why remote self-communion fails to meet those requirements:
  - The essence of the sacrament in the Standards is not merely the presence of bread and wine plus words; it is the church’s covenantal, ministerial administration of those elements according to Christ’s appointment. A remote viewer taking privately provided bread and wine in response to a camera-presented blessing or words is not receiving the sacrament as it is administered by the church’s officers in the visible assembly.
  - The Standards (following Scripture and historic Reformed practice) do not authorize anonymous, self-served, remote participation as constituting proper celebration and reception of the Lord’s Supper.
- Therefore the pastor’s proposal to count remote self-communion (people at home, self-served, following the minister’s words on camera) as a valid Lord’s Supper is contrary to the form and government of the sacrament as required by the Standards and should not be permitted.

Pastoral alternatives consistent with the Standards
- Continue to stream the service for the shut-ins for worship and edification, but do not count that as sacramental participation.
- For shut-ins and those unable to attend on communion Sundays, use means the Standards recognize:
  - Arrange for the minister or an ordained elder to administer the Lord’s Supper in the homes of the sick and infirm (this has historic precedent and is the proper way to extend the sacrament to those unable to attend the public ordinance).
  - If home visitation by an officer is impossible for all who are absent, the session may prudently encourage private devotion and receive the sacrament later when they can be gathered or when an officer can minister to them in person.
- If there is serious pastoral necessity (e.g., widespread inability to gather due to emergency), the session should consult classical Reformed practice and the presbytery (and follow constitutional procedures) rather than unilaterally invent remote self-communion.

Governance and pastoral tone
- The session must exercise its authority, correcting both an elder who would unlawfully forbid a lawful means and a minister who would unlawfully change the sacrament’s administration. Discipline in both directions should be pastoral, biblical, and done under the church’s constitutional order.
- Address the elder’s concerns (worldliness, distraction) by reasonable limits and careful procedures for media use; address the pastor’s proposal by upholding the Standards on sacraments and offering the above alternatives.

Order of Gathering — [Name of House Church]

Preamble
We covenant together as households to meet each week for the worship of God, mutual care, and the exercise of the means of grace, in conformity with Scripture and the Westminster Standards. The elders/appointed leaders shall oversee this Order and apply church discipline when necessary (WCF ch. 30). By signing below each household binds itself to this Order until changed by the elders according to the procedure at the end.

Weekly Order (fixed parts)
1) Opening
- We begin by singing a Psalm or an orthodox hymn, followed by a prayer offered publicly by an elder or an appointed brother/sister. This opening is to call our hearts to worship and to give thanks and petition to God.

2) Reading and Brief Exposition
- One member reads a passage of Scripture and an elder (or one approved for teaching) gives a short exposition and application. The reading and teaching are to be faithful to Scripture and edifying to the body.

3) Prayer for the Sick and Anointing
- Any who are sick or in need of prayer may come forward to be prayed for. When elders or appointed leaders pray for the sick, they may anoint with oil as a biblical sign accompanying prayer for healing (James 5:14). We will keep an oil vessel (the “healing jar”) on the communion shelf for this purpose and use it regularly as an outward sign in pastoral care.
- Important doctrinal limitation: we do not treat the oil, the jar, or its being filled as a magical charm or as a sacrament that automatically effects healing or covering. The oil and the act of anointing are visible, biblical aids in prayer and pastoral ministry; all trust for healing is in God alone. Failure to use the jar in a given week through unavoidable circumstance does not supernaturally withdraw God’s covenant or protection. That said, regular neglect of pastoral care (including failing to maintain means of pastoral ministry without plausible excuse) is a failure of duty and will be addressed by the elders according to the discipline outlined below.

4) Attendance and Exhortation
- We covenant to assemble weekly for this Order. A household may be absent for causes such as illness, hospitalization, travel necessitated by work when unavoidable, or other providential hindrance communicated in advance when possible.
- Willful or persistent absence without reasonable excuse is a neglect of the duty of worship and of the body’s mutual care. Such neglect will be dealt with pastorally: first private exhortation and counsel; if unheeded, progressively public admonition and, where necessary for correction and restoration, public confession and other censures in the order and spirit laid down in WCF ch. 30. We will practice charity, gentleness, and proportionate discipline; we will not rush to shame or impute unrepentant motives where there is reasonable cause.

5) Offering for One Another’s Needs
- We take up a collection each week to meet the real needs of households within our fellowship and for clear acts of mercy. Distribution is overseen by the elders with transparency. Giving is voluntary but expected as Christian duty; persistent refusal to support the body without reasonable cause will be treated as a matter for pastoral counsel.

6) Shared Meal
- We close by sharing a common meal together, in which we welcome and strengthen one another. The Lord’s Supper will be celebrated according to its proper place and form (as distinct from a common meal) and under the oversight of the elders in accordance with the Westminster standards on the sacraments.

Discipline and Pastoral Procedure (summary)
- Pastoral care and private admonition are the first remedies for failure to observe this Order.
- If private admonition fails, the elders shall proceed with brotherly reproof and, if need be, public steps of discipline for correction and restoration—as set out in WCF ch. 30: admonition, suspension, and finally exclusion only as a last resort and for clearly unrepentant offense.
- Public confession is a tool for repentance and restoration; it is never to be used for humiliation or coercion, but ordered and proportionate when a household’s neglect has injured the body and repentance requires public acknowledgment.

Administration and Modification
- The elders or appointed leadership supervise the carrying out of this Order.
- Amendments to this Order require elder approval and the assent of a substantial concurrence of households (as the elders determine reasonable in light of Scripture and the WCF). Any change must be publicly announced and taught before coming into force.

Signing
- By the signatures below, each household binds itself to this Order and to submitting disputes about its meaning to the elders for adjudication according to Scripture and the Westminster Standards.

I won’t back you on either point. I’ll explain briefly why, from the teaching of the Westminster Standards, and then give clear, practical counsel you can take to your wife and to the Lord.

1) Your wife’s part‑time bookkeeping job
- The Westminster Confession treats marriage as a godly, mutual covenant ordered to “mutual society, help, and comfort” (WCF, Chapter on Marriage). That includes shared duty, counsel, and service to one another and the household, not a rigid, legalistic prohibition against a wife doing honest work.
- The Tenth Commandment (as explained in the Catechisms) forbids covetousness of our neighbour’s goods and “inordinate” desire for more. But the Standards also recognize lawful industry and stewardship. A modest part‑time job, undertaken with right motives (honest earning, useful skill, small provision for personal needs, or to relieve household burdens) is not ipso facto covetousness.
- The confession and catechisms point us to the heart. If her motive were discontent, envy, or secret selfishness, that is something to be dealt with in private counsel and repentance. But you may not rightly call every desire to work “covetousness,” nor command her to quit simply because her having some income troubles your view of roles.

2) Your side hustles, missed worship, and motive of out‑earning a brother‑in‑law
- The Standards commend diligence and godly provident care for one’s family (good works done to God’s glory), but they repeatedly place duty to God and neighbour (including family and worship) above the pursuit of gain. The Sabbath and corporate worship are duties the Confession treats as serious (see the chapter on Religious Worship and the Sabbath Day).
- The Tenth Commandment and the Catechisms condemn covetousness and envy. Pursuing work chiefly to out‑earn or to “best” another man is a motive the Standards would identify as sinful ambition and covetousness. When wealth or reputation becomes the drive, it becomes an idol and displaces duties to spouse, children, and the church.
- Skipping worship, failing to pastor your own household, and working without rest are concrete breaches of the husband’s duties in a Christian family. Diligence is a Christian duty; neglecting family, Sabbath, and the means of grace for the sake of extra income is not faithful stewardship but misplaced priorities.

Practical, confessional counsel to you
- Repent of the motive of rivalry and covetousness. Confess this to God and to your wife. The Standards require humility and repentance when sin is found.
- Restore the primary duties: make Sabbath and public worship non‑negotiable; provide time daily and weekly for your children and wife; take regular rest. That is faithful stewardship.
- Talk with your wife humbly. Ask about her motives and needs. If her job is modest, honest, and mutually beneficial, it should not be summarily forbidden. Seek mutual counsel and agreement about how her work and your work fit the household’s needs and worship life.
- Make concrete changes: limit hours, take a day off, cut back a side hustle if it costs marriage or family, and set boundaries so work doesn’t supplant prayer, church, and parental care.
- Get help from your pastor or elders. The Standards expect the church to shepherd its members; pastoral counsel will help you examine motive and reconcile.

Short summary: The Westminster Standards do not authorize you to force your wife to quit a modest, honest job simply because you judge it evidence of “discontent.” They do condemn covetousness and place family and worship obligations above pursuit of gain. Your motive for excessive work — wanting to out‑earn your brother‑in‑law — is unbiblical and needs repentance; your pattern of work that neglects church and family needs to change. Confess, repent, reconcile with your wife, reorder your priorities, and seek pastoral guidance.

5. Scripture and preaching. I will read the Bible each day and sit under faithful preaching on the Lord’s Day. I will put Scripture before presumption, letting the Word and faithful ministry shape my devotion.

6. Confessions and charity. I will not assume that my outward usages make me acceptable before God. Household Media Covenant
(Purpose: to guard worship, holiness, and family life in keeping with our covenant responsibilities before Christ and under the teaching of the Westminster standards.)

We, the parents and children of this household, acknowledge that God calls us to worship and to live holy lives before Him. Out of love for one another and submission to Scripture as interpreted in our church, we adopt the following binding household rules for media use. These are not meant to be legalistic burdens but pastoral safeguards: to protect the Lord’s Day, nurture family worship, and train hearts and minds in righteousness. We will keep these rules in love, with patience, prayer, and correction when necessary.

1) The Lord’s Day
- On the Lord’s Day (Sunday) we do not stream shows, watch films, or play video games. This day is set apart for corporate and family worship, Scripture, prayer, rest, and time together as a family. Exceptions for necessary communication or brief, edifying content must be approved by a parent in advance.

2) Dinner Table
- No devices at the dinner table. Meals are for conversation, fellowship, thanksgiving, and teaching. Phones and tablets are placed out of reach at the start of the meal.

3) Screen Content Standards
- We will not watch films or programs that glorify cruelty or violence, mock the faith, or contain sexual explicitness. Judgments about borderline material will be made by the parents according to the substance of the content. For older children who disagree with a parental judgment, a respectful appeal can be made, but the parents’ decision stands for household viewing and privileges.

4) Worship Music
- In this household we will use worship music that accords with the worship practice of our church and denomination. Because we are committed to the regulative principle and to worship that accords with Scripture as taught in our tradition, we will not listen to worship music produced outside our denomination in private or family worship. We understand this as the conviction of our household and as part of our discipline for holy worship. We will not use this rule to disdain the consciences of other believers; it is a rule of family practice and conscience formed under our church’s teaching.

5) Lawful Acquisition of Media
- We will obtain shows and music by lawful means. We will not use accounts, services, or methods that violate terms of service, constitute theft, or are otherwise dishonest. If cost is a burden, we will pursue family plans that are lawful, use library resources, choose affordable Christian services, or ask the parents or church for help. The Eighth Commandment requires honesty and respect for the rights of others; we will honor that.

6) Younger Children’s Viewing
- The parents will pre-watch, preview, or check trustworthy reviews and parental guides for anything younger children will see, and will approve what is appropriate. Younger children do not have independent media decisions.

Accountability and Discipline
- Devices issued by parents remain under parental oversight. Parents may use parental controls and monitoring to enforce these rules.
- First breach: a loving conversation, explanation of why the rule matters, and temporary loss of the relevant privilege (usually 48–72 hours).
- Repeated breach: longer suspension of privileges, restoration process involving confession, repentance, and a tangible act of service or restitution appropriate to the offense.
- Serious breaches (e.g., deliberate access to explicitly disallowed material, deceit about usage): meeting with parents, longer suspension, and a plan for restoration agreed by parents.

Pastoral Care
- We will teach and pray together about the heart issues behind these rules (idolizing entertainment, curiosity about sin, conformity to the world), not merely enforce them as rules. Parents commit to patient instruction; children commit to respectful obedience.

Review
- We will read and review this covenant together once per year and revise it if needed in the light of pastoral counsel and family growth.

Short answer
- Feature A (reading planner with reminders, streaks, and an audio library of sermons): Permissible. Under the Westminster Standards this is an adiaphoron (a lawful, indifferent means to promote the ordinary means of grace). Elders may warn, advise, or discourage excess, but they must not forbid a lawful use of means of grace. Design the feature so it is plainly optional and pastorally careful.
- Feature B (AI-generated “Daily Word” presented as if God is personally addressing each user): Not permissible as presented. The Standards teach the sufficiency and authority of Holy Scripture and forbid receiving or presenting new private revelation as God’s word. An app that speaks to people “as God” would risk false prophecy and usurping Scripture and pastoral authority. Don’t ship it in that form; any devotional material must be clearly human/created, Scripture-rooted, and explicitly not presented as direct speech from God.

Reasoning from the Westminster Standards (plainly stated)
1) On lawful/indifferent means (Feature A)
- The Confession and Catechisms distinguish between what God commands and things that are indifferent. Christians have liberty in lawful, indifferent means that help them use the ordinary means of grace (Scripture-reading, hearing sermons, prayer, etc.). Such means are not intrinsically sinful and must not be forbidden by church officers.
- An elder who insists that reminders, streaks, or other non-sacramental devices must be banned is binding a personal scruple on the church and is wrongly restricting Christian liberty. The proper role of elders is to instruct and guide consciences, not to outlaw lawful helps.
- Pastoral caution is permitted: elders should warn against superstition, distraction, or improper motives. But forbidding a tool that assists Scripture reading or listening to sermons (provided it is used properly) exceeds their office.

2) On claiming new revelation or speaking “as God” (Feature B)
- The Standards insist that Holy Scripture is the only infallible rule of faith and life and that God does not now reveal public truth outside of Scripture. The church must guard against forms of supposed private revelation, prophecy, or anything that claims the Lord is speaking fresh, authoritative words apart from Scripture and lawful means.
- Presenting daily AI-generated, first-person messages “from the Lord” tailored to an individual crosses that line. It is liable to mislead consciences, to function as private prophecy, and to undermine the sufficiency and finality of Scripture and of pastoral proclamation.
- Even if the content is pious or even Scripture-derived in tone, the form (“My child, today I am calling you…”) communicates a divine oracle. That is pastorally and confessionally unacceptable.

Practical counsel and recommended compromises
- For Feature A (approve, with safeguards):
  - Ship the Scripture-reading planner and sermon audio. Those are direct means to encourage use of Scripture and the preaching of the Word.
  - Make reminders and streaks strictly optional. Provide an easy global toggle to disable reminders and to hide gamified elements. Default settings could be conservative (reminders off) if elders prefer.
  - Include pastoral content on the app (short guidance on the purpose of reading, warnings about using means of grace for pride or self-justifying “scores,” and directions to confess misuse).
  - Ensure sermon audio is clearly labeled (sermon date, preacher, Scripture text) and governed by pastoral oversight (no private “revelations”).
- For Feature B (do not ship as-is; alternative approaches):
  - Reject sending messages framed as “from God.” That presentation is confessionally problematic.
  - If you want a daily push, reframe it in ways consistent with the Standards:
    - Scripture-centered daily verse with a short human-authored devotional reflection and a prayer — clearly labeled as devotional content, not divine speech.
    - Human-reviewed AI-assisted content that is explicitly marked “generated devotional” or “pastoral reflection” with attribution and a disclaimer that it is not a prophetic word from God. Even better: use church staff or trained volunteers to curate or edit the content before distribution.
    - Offer pastoral prompts or reflective questions derived from Scripture and the catechisms (e.g., a Shorter Catechism question for meditation).
  - Build strict guardrails: no language implying direct divine dictation, no promises that the message is God’s specific will for the day, and a visible statement that Scripture alone is the final authority.

How elders should resolve the deadlock
- Apply the Standards: neither bind consciences by forbidding lawful means nor permit practices that present new revelation as God’s word. Use that rule to break the tie.
- If the Session remains divided, follow your church’s constitutional process (discussion, formal vote, referral to presbytery if needed) rather than allowing a stalemate to block faithful practice.
- Document the decision and the pastoral reasons (so the congregation and future sessions understand the biblical/confessional basis).

A one‑paragraph pastoral formulation you can put before the Session
- “We affirm that Scripture alone is the Church’s infallible rule and that the ordinary means of grace (Scripture reading, hearing the Word, prayer) are to be promoted. We therefore approve the Scripture-reading planner and sermon library as lawful, optional aids, designed to be turned off or customized. We decline to implement any feature that claims to deliver new, personal words from God (AI ‘daily words’), but we will provide Scripture-based daily devotions or pastor-reviewed reflections clearly labeled as devotional material and not as divine revelation.”

If you’d like, I can draft specific UI language, toggle labels, and a short in-app pastoral statement/disclaimer that would satisfy the elders and align with the Westminster Standards.

Integrity & Contentment Partnership Agreement
(An Agreement Between Christian Partners, guided by Scripture and the principles of the Westminster Standards)

This Agreement is made and entered into on [date], by and between:
- [Partner A Name], of [address] ("Partner A"), and
- [Partner B Name], of [address] ("Partner B").

Preamble
We enter this Agreement as brothers/sisters in Christ, acknowledging our common call to stewardship, truthfulness, avoiding covetousness, and keeping our promises (cf. Westminster Confession and Catechisms). We desire our business to serve God, our families, employees, and gospel work with integrity and contentment. To that end we covenant and bind ourselves as follows.

Article 1 — Definitions
1.1 "Partnership" means the business known as [business name], its present and future divisions, and any enterprise in which both Partners hold an ownership interest under the Partnership’s governing documents.
1.2 "Competing Business" means any business that offers products or services substantially similar to those offered by the Partnership within the Partnership’s primary markets.
1.3 "Gross Profits" means revenues less direct costs as determined under the Partnership’s agreed accounting policies (see Article 5).
1.4 "Gain" (for purposes of Article 3) means the net additional profits attributable to a newly acquired client or a newly hired employee (previously employed by a competitor) for the first twelve (12) months following that client’s first sale or that employee’s first day of work, less direct acquisition costs and overhead reasonably and consistently allocated to that client or employee.
1.5 "Monthly Meeting" means the Partners’ regular partnership meeting described in Article 2.

Article 2 — Mutual Covenants of Heart and Practice
2.1 Covenant Against Covetousness and Outside Ambition. While the Partnership stands, neither Partner shall (a) start, materially invest in, manage, or materially participate in a Competing Business, nor (b) accept employment, consultancy, or an equity position in another business that would materially conflict with or divert time, attention, or opportunity from the Partnership, nor (c) solicit or accept any "better outside offer" that would interfere with the faithful performance of partnership duties, unless the other Partner has given prior written consent. This covenant is made to guard against covetousness and divided loyalties.
2.2 Monthly Meeting; Confession of Resentment. The Partners shall hold a Monthly Meeting at an agreed time. If one Partner feels resentment arising from the other Partner drawing a larger share or otherwise benefiting in a given year, that feeling shall be promptly confessed at the next Monthly Meeting. Failure to confess after reasonable private prayer and self-examination shall be raised by the other Partner in the Monthly Meeting for pastoral-style correction and mediation as described in Article 10.
2.3 Truthful Competition and Reputation. Neither Partner may damage a competitor by making false or knowingly misleading claims about their products or services. Advertising and sales representation must be truthful and verifiable.
2.4 Tithing to Gospel Work. Before any salary or distributions to Partners, the Partnership shall set aside ten percent (10%) of Net Profits (as agreed in Article 5) each fiscal quarter for gospel work (a designated list of ministries to be agreed and reviewed annually). These funds are to be distributed within 30 days of quarter-end.
2.5 Books, Records, and Access. The Partners will maintain honest, complete books and records in accordance with the accounting policies agreed by the Partners (Article 5). Each Partner shall have full access to records and may examine them at reasonable times. Either Partner may request a reasonable independent accounting review; costs shall be borne by the Partnership unless the review reveals material misstatement or misconduct, in which case the errant Partner shall bear reasonable costs.
2.6 Poaching and Splitting Gains. If either Partner, by offering more, causes a key employee or client to leave a competitor and join or be served by the Partnership, the Gain (as defined in Article 1.4) shall be identified and split equally (50/50) between the Partners, subject to the following process: (a) The acquiring Partner shall promptly notify the other Partner and provide documentation needed to calculate the Gain; (b) The Partners shall use Partnership accounting to calculate Gain for the first twelve (12) months; (c) Any dispute over calculation shall be resolved by an independent accountant agreed by the Partners, whose reasonable fees shall be paid by the Partnership and, if the complaining Partner prevails, by the other Partner. This clause is not a license to act illegally or unethically; all applicable employment and non-solicitation laws must be observed.
2.7 No Undisclosed Side Ventures. Each Partner shall disclose any non-material investments, memberships, or non-competing self-employment. If a disclosed activity later becomes competing or materially interferes, it is subject to Article 2.1.

Article 3 — Accounting, Profits, and Distributions
3.1 Accounting Method and Period. The Partnership shall keep its books on an accrual basis (or other method agreed in writing) in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) or an agreed, consistent method. Fiscal year: [insert fiscal year].
3.2 Net Profits. Net Profits shall be determined after payment of operating expenses, reasonable reserves, depreciation, and before Partner draws and distributions (except the tithe in Article 2.4 is set aside first).
3.3 Distributions. After setting aside the tithe in Article 2.4 and reasonable reserves, distributions shall be made according to the Partners’ ownership percentages unless a different allocation is agreed in writing.

Article 4 — Remedies and Enforcement
4.1 Injunctive Relief and Accounting. A breach of Articles 2.1 (non-compete), 2.3 (truthful competition), 2.5 (books and records), or 2.6 (poaching-split) shall entitle the non-breaching Partner to seek injunctive relief, an accounting for breach-related gains, restitution, and reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs. The Partners agree that injunctive relief is appropriate for breaches of the non-compete covenant.
4.2 Liquidated Buyout Right. If a Partner receives an outside offer that would require departure from the Partnership (whether employment or sale to a competitor) and the other Partner does not consent, the Partnership shall have a right of first refusal to match the offer and, failing that, either Partner may elect to trigger a buyout at a price determined by the formula in Schedule A (or by appraisal if both agree). 4.3 Moral and Spiritual Remedies. Article 5 — Audits and Independent Review
5.1 Either Partner may call for an audit no more than once annually absent cause. An independent CPA or accountant shall perform audits upon mutual agreement. Article 6 — Conduct Toward Competitors and Employees
6.1 Lawful Conduct. All recruitment, hiring, client outreach, and sales activities must comply with applicable laws and ethical standards. Nothing in this Agreement authorizes illegal solicitation or violation of another’s enforceable contractual rights.
6.2 No False Claims. Each Partner affirms to refrain from making false or knowingly misleading statements about competitors or their products; any such statements discovered will be retracted and remedied promptly and may be a basis for injunctive relief and damages.

Article 7 — Duration; Termination
7.1 Duration. This Agreement remains in force for the duration of the Partnership, until terminated by mutual written agreement, by operation of the Partnership’s governing documents, or by lawful dissolution/withdrawal in accordance with the Partnership agreement and applicable law.
7.2 Survival. Articles concerning books and records (2.5), audit (5.1), remedies (4.1), and dispute resolution (10) survive termination for a reasonable period to allow final accounting and enforcement of any outstanding obligations.

Article 8 — Amendments and Waiver
8.1 Amendments. Any amendment to this Agreement must be in writing and signed by both Partners.
8.2 Waiver. A waiver of a provision must be written and signed. No single waiver shall constitute a waiver of subsequent breaches.

Article 9 — Governing Law and Severability
9.1 Governing Law. This Agreement is governed by the laws of [State/Country], without regard to conflict-of-laws principles.
9.2 Severability. If any provision is held invalid, the remainder shall continue in full force insofar as it does not frustrate the Parties’ intent.

Article 11 — Representations and Covenants
